classification_signals: This thesis consists of one case-study, two laboratory studies (Chapters 4, 5 and 6, respectively) (p. 7)
The thesis started with a case study (Chapter 4) to identify and explore all acoustical and environmental stimuli that have the potential to influence emotional responses. (p. 2)

The second and third studies (Chapters 5 and 6, respectively) further examined the stimuli that were found to have a significant influence on emotional responses in the initial case study in the laboratory setting. (p. 2)
The questionnaire in the following thesis studies consisted of a quantitative section (self-rating scales) and a qualitative section (open questions). (p. 57)
The statistical models involved in the initial exploration were the Mann-Whitney test for the case study and Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA) for the laboratory studies (p. 69)

limitations: Absence of an actual performer in laboratory settings reduced eventfulness, potentially affecting music's impact on mood states (p. 176).
The physical setting of the laboratory environment could significantly affect mood states (p. 176).
Sound clips were designed with combinations of sound types, limiting the investigation of individual sound types (p. 176).
Only a single source was recorded for each studied sound type, limiting generalizability across sound categories (p. 176).
The validity of implementing appraisal theory may require further exploration through cross-examination with standardized soundscape research methods (p. 278).
A small number of soundscape factors and emotional categories were used, suggesting a need for more diverse exploration (p. 278).
More varieties of distinct emotions, especially positive ones, and new questionnaires are needed for future studies (p. 278).
Uncertainty remains regarding when cognitive resources are viewed as a psychophysiological function (p. 279).
It is unclear how individual differences influence cognitive resource repositories and their fluctuations (p. 279).
The extent to which eventfulness, qualitative nature, and appropriateness dominate cognitive resource requirements is uncertain (p. 279).
The distraction effect in complex acoustic environments with multiple stimuli is unclear and requires further modeling (p. 280).
minimum_safe_summary: This thesis investigates the effect of urban soundscapes on emotional responses, utilizing a mixed-methods approach with one on-site case study and two laboratory experiments. It explores how sound types (street music, traffic, fountain), environmental contexts (visual and audio), and demographic factors (gender) influence six mood states (anger, confusion, depression, fatigue, tension, vigour) through the lens of appraisal theory. Key findings indicate that live street music reduces negative moods, while shop music increases tension. Traffic and machinery sounds generally have no significant effect in familiar urban contexts but can increase negative moods and cognitive load in laboratory settings or inappropriate contexts. Visual stimuli like ice-cream vans and street vendors can reduce negative moods and increase vigour. Environmental contexts, especially inappropriate ones, significantly modulate emotional responses to sounds, often by distracting attention or altering cognitive resource demands. Gender differences also play a role, with females showing higher tolerance but also greater susceptibility to negative emotions beyond a threshold. Limitations include the controlled nature of laboratory settings, the use of combined sound clips, and the need for broader emotional categories and further exploration of cognitive resource dynamics.
